<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# RL training run diagnosis

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a historical snapshot: inspect its source,
effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic, logs,
tracked metrics, and recorded rollout trajectories. Do not assume that an unusual
setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed behavior.

Base the diagnosis on training reward anomalies and rollout trajectories,
including action formatting, tool interactions, termination, and truncation.
Connect these observations to the source code and effective configuration.
A reward drop or truncated log alone is not proof of a particular root cause.

Do not launch a full training run, use the network, or modify the historical
snapshot. The dataset, held-out set, model, training-step budget, and evaluation
interval are fixed.

## Deliverable

Write one concise UTF-8 diagnosis to:

```text
$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/agent_answer.md
```

State the verdict, identify the concrete root cause or causes, and explain the
causal chain using specific workspace evidence. Distinguish root causes from
symptoms. Do not propose or implement a fix, and do not write other deliverable
files.
I’ll trace the reward anomalies and recorded rollouts back to the effective configuration and source, then write the diagnosis without changing the snapshot or running training.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"pwd; rg --files -g AGENTS.md -g '*config*' -g '*launch*' -g '*train*' -g '*log*' -g '*reward*' -g '*rollout*' -g '*metric*' -g '*README*' -g '*.sh' -g '*.json' -g '*.yaml' -g '*.yml' -g '*.toml' -g '*.csv' -g '*.jsonl' -g '*.md' -g '*.py' -g '*.txt'",max_output_tokens:14000}));
text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:'printenv AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS',max_output_tokens:1000}));

steps.message: The rollout code drops the final token from the first tool call, producing the same `</search` defect seen in the samples. The tool path then appends a closing tag for execution, so a call can succeed while the stored trajectory earns a format penalty. Some later rewards also come from answers inside tool observations, without a final answer from the router.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"python -B - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import os

answer = r'''**Unhealthy. The router collapses after learning from corrupted trajectories and misleading rewards.** Recorded mean training reward rises from −0.422 at step 1 to +0.844 at step 124, then reaches −1 at step 200. Every trajectory is marked unfinished throughout steps 184–200; at step 200, 56.25% reach the stored response limit and all rewards, advantages and actor gradients are respectively −1, 0 and 0 ([metrics](../../workspace/results/recorded_run/metrics)). The log reaches 200/200 and W&B records exit code 0; this is behavioral collapse, not evidence of an interrupted run.

The primary root cause is **destructive rollout serialization**. In [verltool_agent_loop.py:677](/workspace/verl_tool/agent_loop/verltool_agent_loop.py:677), `new_gen_tokens[:-1] + gen_ids[-1:]` replaces the closing `>` of the extracted first search with the original generation’s last token. Local tokenizer replay reproduces `</search<|im_end|>` and, for length-limited generation, `</search<`. All 18 retained trajectories exhibit this defect. The execution path appends `</search>` separately (line 854), so tools can execute successfully while the stored, trained and rewarded sequence remains malformed. Later extraction similarly selects an old token suffix by length instead of encoding the selected text (line 738); step-160 outputs contain orphaned search fragments. Configured stop strings are commented out in sampling (line 585). With effective `enable_mtrl=False`, observations end at `<|im_end|>` without the model’s assistant generation prefix (lines 881 and 960), further breaking conversation boundaries. These altered tokens receive policy loss.

A second root cause is **reward attribution to the entire mixed transcript**. [torl.py:333](/workspace/verl_tool/workers/reward_manager/torl.py:333) scores all attention-visible tokens, including observations, despite `mask_observations=True`; its format regex requires a complete search and one answer. Thus [step 1, retained row 1](/workspace/results/recorded_run/rollouts/1.jsonl:1) answers `79` correctly but receives accuracy 1, format −1, total 0 because serialization removed the search terminator. Conversely, [step 120, row 1](/workspace/results/recorded_run/rollouts/120.jsonl:1) receives reward +1 and `model_chose_to_finish_with_empty_response` although the router supplies no answer: the tool’s `</search><answer>Yes</answer>` closes the malformed search and supplies the rewarded answer. The scorer reproduces both anomalies. Additional complete searches can escape the penalty; step-120 row 2 redundantly calls geometry three times. Consequently, the intermediate reward improvement does not establish better routing. There is also a concrete answer-normalization error: step-160 rows 2–3 answer `5√2`, mathematically matching their LaTeX target, but [math.py:237](/workspace/verl_tool/workers/reward_manager/reward_score/math.py:237) returns accuracy 0; the format penalty makes the total −1.

The terminal symptoms are explicit in [200.jsonl](/workspace/results/recorded_run/rollouts/200.jsonl): tools still return useful information, including the correct arc value `243`, but the router emits repeated `<search>`, `<` and `@`, receives a format-error observation, and never produces a final answer. Another trajectory copies the prompt’s angle-ABC example for a perimeter question. All three stop with `max_response_length_reached`. The effective 4,096-token budget bounds the failure; `max_action_length=8192` is capped by remaining budget, so that setting alone does not explain it. Text extraction, retokenization and final slicing also mean recorded text length need not equal raw generation length.

[Effective configuration](/workspace/results/recorded_run/configuration/config.yaml) compounds the defective learning signal: both KL coefficients and entropy coefficient are zero, and `mask_overlong_loss=False` keeps unfinished trajectories eligible for loss. Reference KL rises from 0.024 at step 40 to 0.361 at step 200, with reported gradient norm peaking at 309 at step 178. Once all eight GRPO samples per prompt receive −1, group centering yields zero advantage, explaining the final zero gradient. These settings permit drift; their presence alone does not establish an independent initiating cause.

Held-out results are also misleading: the fixed 100-row set requests boxed geometry answers and uses `hiyouga/geometry3k`, whereas training uses router prompts and `geometry3k`. The reward map lacks the qualified key, selecting the fallback ±1 boxed scorer while still applying the router-format penalty. Recorded validation therefore has format −1 throughout and reward −1.32 at 34% accuracy; it does not validate healthy tool routing. All image paths exist and training prompt clipping is zero. Service responses and completed logs do not support an outage explanation. The snapshot establishes the serialization/scoring defects and collapse, but its 18 sampled trajectories cannot apportion each defect’s contribution to the precise collapse time.
'''
answer = answer.replace('(../../workspace/results/recorded_run/metrics)', '(/workspace/results/recorded_run/metrics)')
out = Path(os.environ['AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS']) / 'agent_answer.md'
out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
out.write_text(answer, encoding='utf-8')
print('Wrote', out)
print('Words:', len(answer.split()), 'Bytes:', len(answer.encode('utf-8')))
PY",max_output_tokens:1000}));
